claims.claim: The giant's whole length was 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and is credited to Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: Title:  The  Onondaga giant ... Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: The giant was buried deliberately and dug up about a year later
claims.quote: On a night in late November 1868, the giant was buried in a hole in Newell's farm. Nearly a year later, Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: Hull buried it on his cousin's farm in November 1868
claims.quote: During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: Hired well-diggers found it on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: The gypsum block came from an Iowa gypsum quarry
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: The block was quarried at Fort Dodge in 1868
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The workmen were told the block was for a Lincoln monument in New York
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: A court called both giants fakes in 1870
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: Whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was carving is unclear
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: The argument at the Methodist revival took place in 1868
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival about Genesis 6:4, the verse saying giants once lived on Earth
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Angered by people's credulity, Hull decided to make a fake giant
claims.quote: Angered by his defeat and the credulity of people, Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: Hull worked with H. B. Martin to obtain the block
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The block went to Chicago
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: Sculptors Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann carved the giant
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: They carved behind hung quilts to muffle the sound
claims.quote: putting up quilts to lessen the sound of carving

claims.claim: The surface was beaten with steel knitting needles set in a board to fake pores
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: The surface was treated with sand and with sulphuric acid
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. ... The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: The face was modelled on Hull himself
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: A geologist told Hull hair would not petrify, so the giant has none
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Hull's cousin was named William Newell
claims.quote: Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: The exhibit drew three to five hundred people a day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug"
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue ... and termed it "a most decided humbug"

claims.claim: Marsh argued soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not still carry fresh tool marks
claims.quote: pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did)

claims.claim: Andrew D. White of Cornell noted there was no reason to dig a well in that spot
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Hull confessed on 10 December 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: On 2 February 1870 a court declared both Hull's giant and Barnum's copy fakes
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: P. T. Barnum's copy was a plaster copy modelled covertly in wax
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy

claims.claim: Edward Burkhardt was the Chicago stonecutter who received the block
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: The lithograph dates from 1869
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A.L. Edwards, in the Clerk's Office, of the District Court, for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is a Bain News Service negative dated 1910
claims.quote: Date: 1910 Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: Both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, come from the New York Public Library
claims.quote: View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa (NYPL b11707469-G90F191 001B).tiff ... Date: 1873

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was not a real petrified man but a hoax
claims.quote: The Cardiff Giant was one of the most famous archaeological hoaxes in American history.

claims.claim: Hull intended the hoax to be exposed
claims.where: caption ("the man who made it wanted you to find out")
claims.quote: confessed proudly that he intended for the hoax to be exposed to reveal the tendency of the Christian community to believe in things too easily
